analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination against people with disabilities in jobs, government services, transportation, and public businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote of its own, but its language was carried into companion bill H.R. 2273, which became the Americans with Disabilities Act covering an estimated 43 million Americans.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban discrimination against people with disabilities in four areas: hiring and employment at companies with 15 or more workers, state and local government services and public transportation, privately owned places the public uses such as restaurants and stores, and telephone service, which would have to include 24-hour relay lines for deaf and speech-impaired callers. Businesses and transit agencies would have to make changes, but only up to defined cost limits. The bill never came up for a vote on its own; its content was carried forward in a companion bill, H.R. 2273, which became the Americans with Disabilities Act later in 1990.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's own findings put the number of Americans with disabilities at about 43 million [S3]. They would gain enforceable protections in four areas: an employment ban on disability discrimination by employers with 15 or more workers, with a right to reasonable accommodation unless it poses an undue hardship [S2][S3]; equal access to state and local government services and to public transportation, including accessible new buses and rail cars, complementary paratransit, and retrofits of key stations [S2][S3]; access to privately run places of public accommodation such as restaurants, stores, hotels, doctors' offices, and theaters [S2][S3]; and 24-hour telephone relay services for people with hearing or speech impairments, priced no higher than ordinary calls [S2]. People who had faced discrimination with no legal recourse would gain the enforcement powers and remedies of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal for employers with 15 or more employees to discriminate against qualified workers with disabilities in hiring, firing, pay, promotion, and training, and requires reasonable accommodations unless doing so would be an undue hardship.

Guarantees people with disabilities equal access to state and local government services and programs, with the enforcement remedies of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 available to anyone facing discrimination.

Requires that new buses and rail cars be accessible, that rail systems provide complementary paratransit for people who cannot use fixed-route buses, and that key rail stations be made accessible within set deadlines.

Opens privately owned restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, doctors' offices, and similar businesses to people with disabilities, with the Attorney General empowered to sue over patterns of discrimination.
Requires telephone companies to provide 24-hour-a-day relay services so deaf and speech-impaired people can communicate by phone at rates no higher than voice calls.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees would bear the cost of reasonable accommodations and face the same enforcement machinery as under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 [S2][S3]. Businesses open to the public — restaurants, stores, hotels, theaters, doctors' offices — would have to remove barriers where it is "readily achievable" and make new construction accessible [S3]. Public transit agencies would have to buy accessible vehicles, run complementary paratransit service, and retrofit key rail stations, with cost-based exemptions for undue financial burden [S3]. Telephone companies would have to provide round-the-clock relay services for deaf and speech-impaired callers at rates no higher than voice service [S2].

drawbacks.text: The employment protections apply only to employers with 15 or more employees (25 for the first two years after enactment), leaving workers at smaller firms uncovered.

People currently using illegal drugs are excluded from protection, and the bill explicitly excludes homosexuality, bisexuality, and transvestism from the definition of disability, narrowing who is covered.

Compliance costs fall on businesses and transit agencies — accessible vehicles, paratransit service, and station retrofits are expensive — although the bill scales the burden through the 'undue hardship' and 'readily achievable' standards and allows deadline extensions of up to 30 years for costly station work.

The bill layers new litigation exposure onto employers and public accommodations, borrowing the remedies of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and authorizing attorney's fees, which critics of the later law have argued invites disputes over accommodation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad and durable: legal recourse against discrimination for tens of millions of people who previously had none, plus concrete access to jobs, buses and trains, stores, and phone service. The costs are real but deliberately scaled — employers only cover firms above 15 workers, accommodations can be refused for undue hardship, businesses only remove barriers that are 'readily achievable,' transit deadlines stretch up to 30 years for costly retrofits, and paratransit can be limited by financial burden. The main design criticism is that the narrow disability definition and the small-employer exemption leave out real populations, not that the costs are unlimited.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never came to a floor vote on its own — a few weeks after introduction, the House record redirected it to a companion bill, H.R. 2273, which became the Americans with Disabilities Act signed into law in July 1990.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 14, 1990 by Rep. Steny Hoyer with a bipartisan list of 19 original cosponsors, including Republicans Newt Gingrich, Hamilton Fish, and Jim Sensenbrenner.
Because it touched jobs, transit, telecommunications, and House operations, it was referred to six committees, including Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and the Judiciary Committee.
The bill was then sent to subcommittees on Personnel and Police, Civil and Constitutional Rights, Surface Transportation, Employment Opportunities, and Select Education.
On May 22, 1990 the House record marked the bill 'For Further Action See H.R.2273,' directing attention to a parallel bill that carried the disability rights legislation forward.

The companion bill became the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, signed into law that July, making the protections drafted here the law of the land despite this bill itself never reaching a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with disabilities came out ahead: the protections drafted in this bill became federal law through the companion bill H.R. 2273, giving roughly 43 million Americans enforceable rights in jobs, transit, public accommodations, and telecommunications.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with disabilities, through the companion bill

for.name: Rep. Steny Hoyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors across six committees' jurisdiction

for.name: 7 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the original sponsor list included Newt Gingrich, Hamilton Fish, Jim Sensenbrenner, Steve Gunderson, and Bill Rinaldo

for.name: Disability rights organizations and people with disabilities
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for a comprehensive civil rights law covering employment, transit, and public accommodations; their proposals shaped the bill's transportation and enforcement provisions

against.name: Business coalitions including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and small-business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed parts of the accommodation and access mandates during the 1990 negotiations and sought cost limits and phase-ins; the enacted law incorporated scaled standards such as 'undue hardship' and 'readily achievable'

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 12 of 257 House Democrats and 7 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, and the original sponsors included Republicans Newt Gingrich and Hamilton Fish alongside Democrats Steny Hoyer and Tony Coelho-era allies like Jim Sensenbrenner.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retailers, hotels, and other public accommodations
industries.note: Businesses open to the public would have to remove barriers where it is 'readily achievable' and could not refuse service to people with disabilities, but in exchange would gain access to a customer base of some 43 million people with disabilities.

Employers with 15 or more workers would gain a defense when job requirements are 'job related and consistent with business necessity' and would keep the ability to exclude current illegal drug users, while gaining a new obligation to accommodate qualified workers.

Transit agencies would have to buy accessible new vehicles, provide complementary paratransit with an 'undue financial burden' escape valve, and retrofit key rail stations — with deadlines stretchable to 20 or even 30 years for extraordinarily expensive structural changes.

Rail operators would need at least one accessible car per train and accessible new rail cars, but existing stations get up to 20 years to comply and dining cars and commuter cars carry narrower requirements.

Every common carrier would have to provide 24-hour telecommunications relay services for hearing- and speech-impaired callers at rates no higher than voice service, with the FCC overseeing both interstate and intrastate carriers.
The mandate for accessible new construction, alterations, and vehicle retrofits creates a stream of compliance work for contractors, architects, and elevator and lift manufacturers.
